A system prompt is a block of instructions that developers place at the start of every conversation with a language model. It tells the assistant who it is, how formal to sound, and which topics are out of scope. Users usually never see it, which is why some people treat it as a secret.

Security teams advise against relying on that secrecy. Researchers have repeatedly shown that determined users can coax a model into repeating its instructions, so a system prompt should be written as if it could become public. Credentials, customer data and anything legally sensitive belong in separate systems with proper access control.
reference_keypoints: a system prompt holds the developer's standing instructions for role, tone and scope
users usually cannot see it, but it can be coaxed out of the model
credentials and sensitive data should be kept in separate access-controlled systems

Emoji looks like a single picture, but many are built from several code points. The family emoji 👨‍👩‍👧 is made of three separate people joined by an invisible character called the zero-width joiner, which software uses to glue symbols together. If a font does not support the combined shape, it shows the people side by side instead.

The same joiner appears in scripts such as Devanagari and Persian, where it controls how letters connect. Developers should not strip it blindly when cleaning text, because that changes how words look and, in some languages, what they mean.
reference_keypoints: many emoji are sequences of code points joined by the zero-width joiner
unsupported fonts show the parts side by side

The city council voted 7 to 2 on Tuesday to approve a new cycling plan that will add 45 kilometres of protected bike lanes by 2030. The plan, which carries a budget of 62 million euros, prioritises routes connecting the main railway station with the university district and the eastern suburbs.

Supporters argued that the lanes would reduce traffic congestion and improve road safety, pointing to a 28% fall in cyclist injuries in a pilot district last year. Opponents raised concerns about the loss of around 800 on-street parking spaces and the effect on local shops.

Construction of the first phase is scheduled to begin in March next year. The council promised public consultations for each neighbourhood before final designs are approved.
